title: The Last Day
hook: the resurrection, the reckoning, the garden and the fire

segments.voice: Yesterday, rusul, the messengers, and your line: every people had one. Did a stranger or a language you didn't know remind you of it? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-eight.

Tradition says a man in Mecca picked up an old bone, crumbled it in his hand, and asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ a mocking question. Who's going to bring this back to life once it's rotted away? The Qur'an records the question, and the answer that comes back is very short. The one who made it the first time will make it again. That exchange sits near the end of Surah Ya Sin, and tradition links that surah with the dying and the dead. A crumbling bone, a short answer, and the fifth article of faith: the Last Day.
screen: `A CRUMBLING BONE.` → `WHO BRINGS THIS BACK?` → `THE ONE WHO MADE IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: The word for it is akhirah, the hereafter, the life that comes last. The Qur'an keeps setting it beside dunya, this near world, the one we're in now. Belief in the Last Day has four movements. First, the resurrection. The bodies of the dead are raised, the bone in the man's hand included. The answer in Ya Sin is an argument from the first creation: making something again is no harder than making it at all. Second, the reckoning. Every life is laid open. Surah az-Zalzalah, a short surah about the earth shaking, ends with two lines: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then." An atom's weight. Nothing is too small to count, in either direction. Third, the two homes. The Qur'an describes a garden, with rivers, shade and peace, and a fire. It describes both vividly, and it doesn't hide either one. Fourth, the One behind it. In the opening surah, al-Fatiha, Allah is called the Merciful and the master of the Day of Judgment, in the same breath. Mercy and reckoning aren't set against each other in that line; they sit side by side. And this is why the Last Day sits among the six. For Muslims, it gives the ordinary day its weight: the kind word, the shortcut not taken, the atom of good nobody else saw.
screen: `THE BONES ARE RAISED.` · `AN ATOM'S WEIGHT.` · `A GARDEN AND A FIRE.` · then, large: `MERCIFUL, AND MASTER OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: think of meeting Him, or, if that's not your language, think of your life being seen whole. Settle, and breathe. Bring up one small good thing from this week, tiny, an atom's weight: a door held, a message answered kindly. Let it be seen. Then one small harm, also tiny. Let that be seen too, without arguing. Hold them both. If you pray, you can recite the opening surah slowly, with its two names: the Merciful, and master of the Day. If you don't, just rest in being seen. The bell holds the time.
Akhirah. The hereafter, the life that comes last: the resurrection, the reckoning, the garden and the fire. The fifth article of faith. Today's word.
Your line: the last day. Today, do one good thing as small as an atom's weight, one nobody else will notice. Tomorrow, the sixth article: the decree. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Belief in the Last Day is the fifth article of faith; Muslims recite al-Fatiha, which names Allah as master of the Day of Judgment, in prayer, and Surah Ya Sin may be read for the dying and the dead.

what it means: the fifth article of faith: resurrection, reckoning to an atom's weight, and the garden and the fire, under the Merciful.
what a scholar hears: the pairing of dunya and akhirah across the Qur'an, and the argument from first creation in Surah Ya Sin.

notes: Hook: the man crumbling a bone is from the tafsir tradition around 36:77–79 (often named as Ubayy ibn Khalaf or al-'As ibn Wa'il); the Qur'an itself records only the question. Consider adding 'tradition says'.
'Muslims often read Ya Sin for the dying and the dead': common practice, a frequency claim; confirm or soften.
'Recited in every unit of prayer' (al-Fatiha in every rak'ah): confirm framing.
Practice phrase 'meeting Him' kept from the outline; offered with an alternative for non-praying listeners.
